newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tax battle is first test for Mexican democracy.
newsitem.headline: Tax battle is first test for Mexican democracy.

text.p: Just weeks after historic congressional elections, Mexico's new-found democracy is being put to the test in a political battle over taxes.

Jubilant at ending the Institutional Revolutionary Party's (PRI) 68-year grip on the lower house of Congress, opposition parties have joined ranks in a determined effort to lower Mexico's 15 percent sales tax.
The tax cut was promised by all four main opposition parties in the run-up to the July 6 vote to an electorate still impoverished by a financial meltdown two years ago.
But the proposal is not simply economic. It also marks the first time opposition parties have mustered enough support on an issue to outgun the PRI in the lower house of Congress.

Instead of bickering as they have in the past, the ideologically-opposed parties have struck a quick consensus on the merits of lowering the tax to 10 percent -- a unity that poses a serious challenge to President Ernesto Zedillo when the new Congress opens on Sept. 1.

"The political cost of blocking the intitiative would be very high," Porfirio Munoz Ledo, lower house leader of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), told Reuters in a recent interview. "There would be gridlock in a week."
In a pre-emptive move, the government and its backers in the business and labour community have issued dire warnings of the perils cutting the tax could entail.
Mexico's most senior tax official, Tomas Ruiz, told reporters on Wednesday it would blow a 25 billion peso ($3 billion) hole in the budget that could not be filled by marginal rises in other taxes.

Other government officials have warned it would be an inflationary or deficit-bloating measure. The country's top business leader, Eduardo Bours, this week raised the specter of a stock market sell-off if the tax is approved.

But their arguments were given short shrift by many Mexicans who viewed the tax as a hated reminder of the 1994-5 economic crisis when the PRI used its congressional majority to pass the rise to 15 percent from 10 percent.

Press photographs of PRI leaders at the time laughing and bragging as they rammed the increase through Congress became anti-PRI campaign posters during the campaign, and analysts say the anti-PRI vote on July 6 was vengeance.

Whether the tax is lowered or not, the debate between the opposition and the government was a refreshing change in Mexico. For decades, the PRI has used its congressional majority to ram through government polices, with little more than token regard for opposition points of view.

The ruling party, which won 239 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies on July 6, could still block the tax cut in the Senate where it retains its majority. But opposition parties have threatened a vigorous counter-attack if it does.

Economists say the benefits of the tax cuts as well as the perils have been overstated, but there are few worries about the implications for the economy. Many say the impact of the tax reduction could be easily offset by spending cuts.
According to Mexican economist Jonathan Heath, investors may actually welcome an opposition victory on the issue as a further sign that democracy is taking hold in Mexico.
"The issue has nothing to do with economics and everything to do with politics," he said.
